title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics

epigraph.quote: A rupee of software revenue is not created equal: if it takes ₹0.23 of capitalized R&D and ₹0.17 of depreciation to deliver ₹0.04 of net profit, the unit economics are running on a treadmill.
epigraph.author: Institutional Field Notes

web_blocks.html: SoftTech sells through two channels: public-sector tendering (G2B) in India and partner-led enterprise sales abroad [3][4]. In India, winning a state building-permit or infra portal (such as AAI or JNPA) takes multi-stage public tenders [4][9]. Bidders must pass technical checks and meet CMMI Level 5 standards [4][9]. Once SoftTech wins a city or state contract, it gains a captive user base [3][17]. Thousands of local architects and builders must use its portal and pre-check tools like RuleBuddy to file plans [3][17].

On the cost side, SoftTech has no physical factory. Its main inputs are software engineers, civil/architectural consultants, cloud hosting, and third-party hardware or GIS licenses [2][6]. Yet the FY26 consolidated accounts reveal a sharp structural flaw in unit economics. Reported P&L expenses understate true cash engineering spend because SoftTech capitalizes a large share of developer payroll [2][6]. Those costs sit inside Intangible Assets Under Development (IAUD) instead of hitting operating expenses [2][6].

web_blocks.takeaway: Out of every ₹100 of revenue, SoftTech generates ₹24.22 in EBITDA, but loses ₹17.18 to amortization and ₹24.51 to ongoing capex/intangibles capitalization, leaving −₹0.99 in Free Cash Flow.

web_blocks.html: The waterfall above shows why SoftTech does not behave like an asset-light software compounder. In FY26, it spent ₹30.50 Cr in cash on 'payments for intangibles development costs' (after ₹34.47 Cr in FY25) [2]. That means SoftTech reinvests 22.9% of its entire FY26 revenue into capitalized internal software work [2]. Suppose those ₹30.50 Cr of development costs had been expensed on the P&L. FY26 EBITDA would drop from +₹32.19 Cr to +₹1.69 Cr, and PBT would turn deeply negative! That accounting choice turns a cash-burning engineering team into a 24.2% EBITDA margin on paper [2]. Owners must look past EBITDA to free cash flow.

Second, working capital stays heavy because government clients pay slowly and demand milestone sign-offs [1][2]. Screener's 'Debtor Days' improved from 167 days (FY25) to 95 days (FY26) as billed receivables fell from ₹43.58 Cr to ₹34.63 Cr [1][2]. However, two balance-sheet items offset that gain. First, ₹53.52 Cr of Contract Assets (unbilled revenue) sits on the books (₹52.79 Cr current plus ₹0.73 Cr non-current) [2]. Second, SoftTech booked ₹12.08 Cr of doubtful-debt provisions and write-offs in FY26 Other Expenses, up 4.3x from ₹2.83 Cr in FY25 [2]. Together, billed receivables and unbilled contract assets total ₹88.15 Cr, or 242 days of FY26 revenue.

This capital intensity also shapes SoftTech's funding mix and credit rating [1][2][19]. Carrying ₹88.15 Cr of billed and unbilled receivables on ₹132.90 Cr of sales strains liquidity [2]. To bridge that gap, SoftTech holds ₹28.27 Cr in short-term debt, ₹3.47 Cr in long-term debt, and ₹7.10 Cr in lease liabilities [2]. Cash and bank balances stood at ₹32.91 Cr at March 31, 2026 [2]. Much of that cash is margin money or pledged deposits for bank guarantees in government tenders [2][19]. CARE Ratings' A3 short-term rating reflects this balance: a solid municipal niche offset by modest scale and slow cash cycles [19].

web_blocks.title: The Capitalization Treadmill
paragraphs: In H1 FY27 (ended September 2026), SoftTech moved ~₹20 Cr from Intangible Assets Under Development into active assets [1]. Fixed and Intangible Assets jumped from ₹81 Cr in March 2026 to ₹111 Cr in September 2026 [1]. Over the same period, CWIP fell from ₹20 Cr to ₹0 Cr [1].

Quarterly Depreciation & Amortization jumped from ₹5.86 Cr in Q4 FY26 to ₹6.84 Cr in Q1 FY27 and ₹6.85 Cr in Q2 FY27 [1]. That equals a ₹27.4 Cr annual non-cash charge [1]. Unless sales grow well past ₹150–180 Cr without adding more capitalized R&D, amortization will keep eating most operating profit.

book_paragraphs: This is the chapter where you and I put on our forensic accountant hats and follow every rupee from the top of the income statement down to the cash register. On the surface, SoftTech's FY26 numbers look encouraging: consolidated revenue jumped nearly 40% to ₹132.90 Cr, and EBITDA was ₹32.19 Cr, a respectable 24.2% margin.

Now let's walk down the ₹100 waterfall together. Out of every ₹100 SoftTech billed in FY26, ₹14.45 went to third-party stock-in-trade, ₹24.82 went to expensed employee salaries, and ₹36.50 went to other operating expenses, which included a sharp ₹12.08 Cr charge for doubtful debts and write-offs. That leaves ₹24.22 in operating profit.

Here is where the magic trick. And the trap, appears. Out of that ₹24.22 of operating profit, ₹17.18 disappears into depreciation and amortization, ₹3.06 goes to interest, and after ₹2.74 of other income and ₹2.71 of tax, only ₹4.01 survives as net profit. Four rupees on a hundred!

And it gets even more revealing when we look at the cash flow statement. Operating cash flow was ₹31.26 Cr, ₹23.52 per ₹100 of sales, because depreciation (₹22.83 Cr) and bad-debt provisions (₹12.08 Cr) are non-cash add-backs. But right below operating cash flow, SoftTech spent ₹32.57 Cr on capex, of which ₹30.50 Cr was cash paid for internal software development! So after paying for its engineers' capitalized code, SoftTech's Free Cash Flow was minus ₹1.31 Cr.

Let's pause and ask a practical question about SoftTech's balance sheet: if the company held ₹32.91 Cr in cash and bank balances at the end of FY26, why did it still carry ₹31.74 Cr of borrowings and pay ₹4.07 Cr in finance costs?

Part of the answer is how government tendering works in India. When you bid for a ₹92.95 Cr port authority contract or a state-wide municipal portal, you have to post earnest money deposits and performance bank guarantees. Notice that out of SoftTech's ₹32.91 Cr cash and bank balance, ₹20.20 Cr sits in 'bank balances other than cash and cash equivalents', typically fixed deposits pledged against bank guarantees and credit lines.

Meanwhile, to bridge the timing gap between paying engineers every month and waiting 242 days for combined billed and unbilled municipal receivables to clear, SoftTech leans on ₹28.27 Cr of short-term working capital debt. That is why CARE Ratings assigns a CARE A3 short-term rating: the business is solvent and liquid thanks to past equity raises, yet its cash cycle remains tight.

Distribution in municipal GovTech is nothing like selling SaaS seats over a website to mid-market US buyers. You cannot run Google Ads to win a state urban-development department. Instead, SoftTech relies on a three-pronged go-to-market engine: (1) direct government tender bidding and empanelment across state urban bodies, (2) a captive ecosystem of thousands of empaneled architects and builders who must use SoftTech's pre-check tools (like RuleBuddy) to avoid municipal rejections, and (3) selective channel and systems-integrator partnerships for larger infrastructure and international bids.

That distribution model creates a structural bottleneck you can see clearly in our ₹100 FY26 revenue-to-free-cash-flow waterfall. Out of every ₹100 of consolidated FY26 revenue (₹132.90 Cr), SoftTech spent roughly ₹75.24 on employee costs and operating expenses, leaving ₹24.76 of EBITDA. Depreciation and amortization consumed ₹17.18 of that ₹24.76, interest took ₹3.17, other income added ₹2.31, and taxes took ₹2.71, leaving just ₹4.01 of statutory net profit per ₹100 of sales.

Now follow the cash below the P&L line. On paper, cash flow from operations (CFO) looked healthy at ₹23.52 per ₹100 of sales (₹31.26 Cr), largely because ₹17.18 of non-cash D&A and ₹9.09 of doubtful-debt provisions are added back to net profit. But immediately below CFO, SoftTech spent ₹24.51 per ₹100 of sales (₹32.57 Cr) on capex and capitalized software development. The net result? Minus ₹0.99 of free cash flow per ₹100 of revenue. Every single rupee generated by operations was consumed by building the next version of the software.

book_callouts.title: The Litmus Test for Capitalized Software
book_callouts.text: Ask yourself: if a software company has to capitalize ₹30.50 Cr of development costs every year just to generate ₹132.90 Cr of revenue and ₹32.19 Cr of EBITDA, is that 'growth capex' or is it actually recurring engineering maintenance disguised on the balance sheet?

book_subsections.title: Unbilled Revenue and the 242-Day Reality
paragraphs: One of the easiest mistakes in Indian GovTech investing is reading a headline ratio like 'Debtor Days improved from 167 to 95' and assuming working capital is fixed. On SoftTech's audited FY26 balance sheet, billed trade receivables indeed fell from ₹43.58 Cr to ₹34.63 Cr.

But look two lines further down under Current Assets: 'Contract Assets', which is accounting language for unbilled revenue where work has been recognized on the P&L before the customer can be formally billed, sat at ₹52.79 Cr, plus ₹0.73 Cr non-current. Put billed receivables (₹34.63 Cr) and unbilled contract assets (₹53.52 Cr) together, and SoftTech had ₹88.15 Cr tied up with customers against ₹132.90 Cr of revenue. That is 242 days of revenue sitting outside the bank.

Even more telling, SoftTech had to write off or provide ₹12.08 Cr for doubtful debts in FY26, more than four times the ₹2.83 Cr provision in FY25. When municipal and government contracts age, not every rupee of recognized revenue turns into cash.

callouts.title: Watch the Q1–Q2 FY27 Depreciation Step-Up
callouts.text: In H1 FY27, SoftTech moved ₹20 Cr out of CWIP/IAUD into active assets, pushing quarterly depreciation to ₹6.85 Cr. Keep your eye on whether new revenue can outrun that ₹27.4 Cr annual amortization wall.

book_subsections.title: Why Pay-Per-Use SaaS Is the Only Escape from the Working-Capital Trap
paragraphs: Think about the unit-economics difference between two ways SoftTech sells the exact same AutoDCR engine. Under the old tender model, a state government signs a ₹15 Cr implementation contract. SoftTech spends 12 months customizing local bye-laws, books revenue as 'Contract Assets' before milestones are signed off, waits another 6 to 12 months for treasury release, and occasionally writes off ₹12 Cr when old balances turn sticky.

Under the newer pay-per-use SaaS model, the municipality mandates online submission, and every time an architect uploads a building plan, the architect or developer pays a scrutiny fee digitally at the portal gate. Cash hits the bank in days, not years, and there is no unbilled contract asset. That is why watching recurring revenue rise from 37.5% to 43.5% of standalone sales is the single most important operational metric in SoftTech's business model.

callouts.title: The Unit-Economics Verdict
callouts.text: SoftTech's unit economics are currently split in two: high-margin, upfront-cash pay-per-use permitting at the core, dragged down by capital-heavy, high-write-off turnkey GovTech and ₹30.50 Cr/year of capitalized software development.

book_subsections.title: Working Capital Friction Inside the Municipal Channel
paragraphs: When you sell software to an Indian municipal corporation or public-sector undertaking, your biggest operational challenge is rarely code deployment, it is treasury collection. Even after a city's town-planning department goes live on AutoDCR or PWIMS, final milestone sign-offs often wait on committee approvals, fiscal-year budget releases, or audit clearances.

That is why SoftTech's FY26 cash-flow statement shows ₹12.08 Cr of credit-loss provisioning and write-offs, more than four times the prior year's ₹2.80 Cr. In effect, roughly 9% of FY26 consolidated revenue had to be provisioned as doubtful or delayed. Until management proves that its new CIVIT cloud billing model can collect cash upfront without accumulating unbilled contract assets, the ₹100 waterfall will continue to leak cash between EBITDA and Free Cash Flow.
